newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore opposition says Goh getting desperate.
newsitem.headline: Singapore opposition says Goh getting desperate.

text.p: Singapore opposition leaders on Tuesday accused the ruling party of smearing their reputations as part of an effort to prevent them from securing landmark gains in Thursday's general election.

Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and leaders of the People's Action Party (PAP) have launched a scathing attack on Workers' Party (WP) candidate Tang Liang Hong, accusing him of harbouring anti-Christian and communal Chinese views in a society that has a long memory of racial riots in the 1960s.
The PAP is already guaranteed a majority in the new 83-member parliament because opposition parties are only contesting 36 seats in the January 2 election.

"My daughter is a Christian. My wife is a Buddhist. I'm a free thinker," Tang declared at a rally of an estimated 5,000 supporters beneath the gleaming high-rises in the heart of Singapore's financial centre. "This is all nonsense."

"The most dangerous thing is to use religion for political identification. That is dangerous," Tang said. "Why are they (the PAP) playing with fire? In short, they are very desperate. They want to stop us from entering parliament."

At the end of the rally a large group of supporters, chanting as they walked, followed Tang and WP secretary-general J.B. Jeyaretnam for a few hundred metres until the two entered a building. Tang was mobbed along the way by admirers.
Goh has staked his prestige on the PAP winning Cheng San, a multi-member constituency in the north of Singapore where Tang and Jeyaretnam are both running for office in the election.

The winning slate gets all five seats at stake and victory for the opposition could more than double their number in parliament if they also retain the four single-member districts they won last time.
Even if the opposition won only the five seats, it would represent an all-time post-independence high in parliament for the opposition.
Goh said on Tuesday that a win for the opposition in Cheng San would hurt him.

"I will be seen as a much smaller man," The New Paper quoted Goh as saying. "As the PM, my word in future will have less weight both internationally as well as in Singapore. I fight to win. I cannot lose."
WP secretary-general Jeyaretnam accused the PAP of smearing the reputations of himself and Tang and trying every tactic to remain in power.
"The election campaign has sunk very low," he said, adding the PAP has launched "a vilification of the opposition candidates, particularly the Workers' Party candidates".
"They fear the WP team from Cheng San more than anything else," Jeyaretnam added. "Reason has fled from their minds. They're so obsessed with the desire to remain in power."

Goh, who leads a party which faced no opposition in parliament for 13 years until Jeyaretnam won a by-election in 1981, has said he is aiming for a clean sweep of all the seats and stemming the recent ebb of votes away from the PAP.
"If the opposition wins eight to 10 seats, it could jeopardise Goh's premiership," said Bruce Gale, analyst at Hong Kong based Political and Economic Risk Consultancy (PERC).
"I don't see that happening...I think the opposition may win as few as two seats, but the PAP is taking no chances," he said.
Chia Woon Khien, economist at Union Bank of Switzerland in Singapore, said she had seen no evidence to suggest the PAP would suffer any major defeat on Thursday.
"I think the PAP's vote will be close to the last election when they got 61 percent of the votes cast," Chia said.
